title: Functionalism and the Computational Mind
subtitle: If minds are what brains do, could something else do it too?
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain functionalism and how it differs from behaviorism and the mind-brain identity theory.
By the end you will be able to state the multiple realizability argument and illustrate it with examples.
By the end you will be able to describe the computational theory of mind and Fodor's language of thought hypothesis.
By the end you will be able to present the inverted spectrum and absent qualia objections, including Block's China Brain, and the main functionalist replies.
hook:
What makes something a mousetrap? Not what it is made of. A classic spring trap is wood and steel; a humane trap is a plastic box with a trapdoor; a sticky trap is cardboard and glue. What they share is a *job*: catching mice. Being a mousetrap is a matter of what a thing does, not what it is made of.

Now ask the same question about pain, belief or desire. On Day 84 you met the puzzles of philosophy of mind: Descartes's dualism (Day 44), Nagel's bat and Chalmers's hard problem. You also met the question of whether a machine could think. This lesson examines the theory that has dominated philosophy of mind and cognitive science since the 1960s, and that makes the idea of a thinking machine seem almost obvious. According to **functionalism**, mental states are like mousetraps: what makes something a pain or a belief is the role it plays, not the stuff it is made of. If that is right, a mind could in principle be built from silicon as well as neurons. Whether it is right is one of the central disputes of modern philosophy.

sections.heading: From Behaviorism and Identity Theory to Function
sections.body:
Functionalism emerged as a solution to the failures of two earlier attempts to fit the mind into a scientific picture of the world.

**Behaviorism**, influential in the mid-twentieth century, held that talk of mental states is really talk of behavior and dispositions to behave. Gilbert Ryle's *The Concept of Mind* (1949) mocked Descartes's dualism as the dogma of the "ghost in the machine." To be thirsty, on a behaviorist analysis, is roughly to be disposed to drink if water is available. The trouble is that mental states produce behavior only in combination with other mental states. A thirsty person who believes the water is poisoned will not drink; a thirsty person who wants to show self-control may refuse. Every attempt to define a single mental state purely in terms of behavior ends up mentioning other mental states. Also, a skilled actor can display pain behavior without pain, and a paralyzed person can feel pain without displaying it.

The **mind-brain identity theory**, developed in the 1950s by U. T. Place ("Is Consciousness a Brain Process?", 1956) and J. J. C. Smart ("Sensations and Brain Processes", 1959), took a bolder line. Mental states simply *are* brain states, just as lightning *is* electrical discharge. The stock philosophers' example was "pain is C-fiber firing" (a simplification; real pain involves many systems). The theory was scientifically respectable and avoided Cartesian ghosts. But it had a problem that soon proved decisive.

If pain just is a certain kind of human neural activity, then any creature without that neural activity cannot be in pain. What about an octopus? Its nervous system is organized very differently from ours, yet it reacts to injury, guards wounds and learns to avoid harm. What about a hypothetical alien with a silicon-based nervous system, or a future robot? The identity theory seems to rule out by definition that they could feel pain, which is, at minimum, presumptuous.

sections.heading: Multiple Realizability and the Functionalist Answer
sections.body:
In a 1967 paper, "Psychological Predicates" (later reprinted as "The Nature of Mental States"), Hilary Putnam turned this problem into an argument. Mental states, he argued, are **multiply realizable**: the same mental state can be realized, or implemented, by very different physical systems. Pain in humans, octopuses and possible Martians might share nothing at the physical level. So pain cannot be identical to any one physical state. Putnam suggested instead that pain is a **functional state** of the whole organism.

A **functional state** is defined by its causal role: by its typical causes, its typical effects, and its relations to other states. Consider a simple vending machine that sells a drink for 50 cents and accepts only quarters. It needs two internal states: S0 ("waiting for 50 cents") and S1 ("waiting for 25 cents").
- In S0, if a quarter is inserted, it moves to S1 and does nothing else.
- In S1, if a quarter is inserted, it dispenses a drink and returns to S0.

That description, a **machine table**, completely specifies what S1 *is*: whatever state plays that role. S1 could be realized by a lever, a magnetic switch or a line of code. Asking "what is S1 made of?" is beside the point.

Functionalism says that mental states are like this, only vastly more complex. Pain is the state that is typically caused by bodily damage, that causes distress and the desire for it to stop, that causes beliefs that something is wrong, and that tends to cause wincing, withdrawal and protective behavior. Any state in any system that plays that role is a pain. A belief that it is raining is the state that is caused by the right perceptions, combines with a desire to stay dry to produce umbrella-taking, and so on.

This solved the problems at a stroke. Unlike behaviorism, functionalism welcomes the interdependence of mental states: each is defined by its place in a network that includes other mental states. (David Lewis showed, in 1970 and 1972, how to define all the states of such a network at once, using a logical technique now called Ramsey-Lewis definition.) Unlike the identity theory, it allows octopuses, Martians and machines to have minds. And unlike dualism, it is fully compatible with physicalism: in us, every functional state is realized by some physical brain state.

Philosophers distinguish varieties. **Machine functionalism** (early Putnam) modeled the mind on a Turing machine table. **Analytic functionalism** (Lewis, David Armstrong) held that our everyday concepts of mental states are concepts of causal roles, discoverable by analyzing folk psychology. **Psychofunctionalism** (Fodor, Pylyshyn) held that the relevant roles are those discovered by scientific psychology.

sections.heading: The Computational Theory of Mind
sections.body:
If mental states are functional states, and functional states can be implemented in computers, then perhaps the mind is a kind of computer. The **computational theory of mind** holds that thinking *is* computation: the manipulation of symbols according to rules.

The idea's most influential defender was Jerry Fodor. In *The Language of Thought* (1975), Fodor argued that thinking takes place in an inner symbolic system, a **language of thought** sometimes called **Mentalese**. When you believe that the cat is on the mat, a mental sentence, built from mental symbols for *cat*, *on* and *mat*, is stored in your belief box, so to speak. Thinking consists in processes that transform such sentences according to their structure.

Why believe this? Fodor offered several arguments.
- **Productivity.** You can think an unlimited number of new thoughts ("a purple giraffe is reading Kant on the Moon"), just as you can understand unlimited new sentences. The best explanation is a finite set of symbols combined by rules.
- **Systematicity.** Anyone who can think that John loves Mary can also think that Mary loves John. Thoughts come in structured families, which suggests they are built from reusable parts.
- **Rationality as computation.** The great insight of Turing (Day 89) was that a machine can perform operations that respect the *meaning* of symbols while being sensitive only to their *shape*, or syntax. A computer adding numbers does not understand numbers, yet its outputs are correct. Fodor argued that this solved an ancient puzzle: how a physical system could reason. If thinking is symbol manipulation, then reasoning can be implemented in a physical mechanism whose transitions preserve truth.

The computational theory shaped the new field of **cognitive science** from the 1960s onward, linking psychology, linguistics (Noam Chomsky's work on grammar), computer science and philosophy. From the 1980s it faced a rival in **connectionism**, which models cognition with networks of simple, neuron-like units that learn by adjusting connection strengths. Fodor and Zenon Pylyshyn argued in 1988 that connectionist networks could not explain systematicity unless they implemented a symbolic system. The debate between symbolic and network approaches has taken a dramatic new turn with today's deep learning systems, which are descendants of connectionism.

sections.heading: Inverted Spectra and Absent Qualia
sections.body:
Functionalism's most serious problems concern consciousness: the felt, qualitative character of experience, or **qualia** (singular, *quale*), such as the redness of red or the hurtfulness of pain.

**The inverted spectrum.** John Locke (Day 47) raised an intriguing possibility in his *Essay Concerning Human Understanding* (1689): what if the color experience a violet produces in one person's mind were the same as the experience a marigold produces in another's, and vice versa? Since both would call violets "violet" and marigolds "yellow," the difference could never be detected. Apply this to functionalism. Imagine someone whose color experiences are systematically inverted relative to yours: where you have the experience of red, she has the experience you have of green. If the inversion is complete, she sorts, names and reacts to colors exactly as you do. Every functional role is the same. Yet her experiences differ. If that is possible, then qualitative experience is not fixed by functional role, and functionalism leaves something out.

**Absent qualia.** Ned Block, in "Troubles with Functionalism" (1978), went further. Suppose the government of China persuades its population (then about a billion people) to simulate your brain's functional organization for an hour. Each citizen is given a two-way radio and instructions: when you receive signals from these people, send a signal to those people. The radios are connected to an artificial body. The whole system now has the same functional organization as your brain, so functionalism says it has your mental states. But does the nation of China, as a whole, feel pain? Many people find it absurd to suppose that the **China Brain** has any experiences at all. If it has the right functional organization but no qualia, then functionalism is false about consciousness.

**Replies.** Functionalists have responded in several ways.
- **Bite the bullet.** Perhaps the China Brain *would* be conscious, and our resistance reflects a bias toward things of familiar size and speed. Our neurons, individually, do not seem conscious either.
- **Deny the possibility.** Sydney Shoemaker (1975) argued that absent qualia are impossible, because qualia make a functional difference: they cause our beliefs about our experiences. A creature whose states had the right roles, including causing beliefs like "I am in pain," could not be missing the pain.
- **Limited functionalism.** Some accept functionalism for beliefs and desires, but not for qualia. This is a widespread position, though it concedes that the hardest part of the mind lies outside the theory.

These objections lead straight into the frontier debates of Lesson 5. And there is a related objection from Searle's Chinese Room (Day 84), which targets not consciousness but understanding: whether symbol manipulation alone could ever amount to meaning.

sections.heading: Where Functionalism Stands Today
sections.body:
Functionalism remains the default framework of cognitive science and probably the most widely held view among philosophers of mind, at least about non-conscious mental states. But it has faced further challenges.

Ironically, Putnam himself abandoned it. In *Representation and Reality* (1988), he argued that any physical system with enough states can be described as implementing almost any machine table, so that being a computation is too cheap to explain the mind. If a rock's molecular jostlings can be mapped onto the states of a word processor, implementation must be constrained. Philosophers since, including David Chalmers, have tried to specify what genuine implementation requires.

Others questioned multiple realizability. William Bechtel and Jennifer Mundale (1999) argued that neuroscience does in fact identify brain areas across species by their similar functions *and* structures, so the evidence for radical multiple realizability is weaker than Putnam thought. And from another direction, defenders of embodied cognition (Lesson 4) argue that the computer analogy overlooks the role of the body and environment in thinking.

Still, functionalism's central insight, that mental states are individuated by what they do, has proven remarkably durable. It lies behind most scientific psychology, and behind the serious question of whether artificial intelligence could ever have a mind.

modernConnection.title: Does a Language Model Believe Anything?
modernConnection.body:
Large language models such as the chatbots now in everyday use have given functionalism its most dramatic test. These systems are trained on enormous amounts of text to predict the next word. They can explain jokes, write code, summarize arguments and answer questions about their own previous answers. Do they have beliefs?

A functionalist must take the question seriously. If a belief is whatever state plays the role of a belief, then the question is not "Is it made of neurons?" but "Does it have internal states that function like beliefs?" Researchers in a field called **mechanistic interpretability** now probe the internal activations of such models and have found evidence of internal representations that track features of the world, such as the layout of a board game in a model that was trained only on lists of moves and never shown the board. That looks like the functional signature of representation.

But there are reasons for caution. A belief, on most functionalist accounts, is integrated with perception, desire and action: it is updated by evidence and guides behavior across many situations. A language model's "beliefs" can be strikingly inconsistent, shifting with how a question is phrased. Emily Bender and Alexander Koller, in a 2020 paper, imagined a hyper-intelligent octopus that taps an undersea cable between two islanders and learns to imitate their messages perfectly, without ever learning what the words refer to. They argued that a system trained only on linguistic form cannot learn meaning. Others respond that meaning may emerge from the structure of relations among words, as functionalism might predict.

And even if functionalism vindicates machine belief, Block's China Brain hangs over the further question of machine experience. A system could have every functional property of belief and still, if the absent qualia objection is right, feel nothing at all. The philosophy of the 1960s and 1970s has turned out to be a direct preparation for some of the most practical questions of the 2020s.

vocabulary.definition: The theory that mental states are defined by their causal roles: their typical causes, effects and relations to other mental states, rather than by what they are made of.
vocabulary.example: A functionalist says pain is whatever state is caused by damage and causes distress and avoidance.

vocabulary.definition: The thesis that the same mental state can be implemented by very different physical systems.
vocabulary.example: If octopuses and humans can both feel pain despite different nervous systems, pain is multiply realizable.

vocabulary.definition: The view that each type of mental state is identical to a type of brain state.
vocabulary.example: The identity theory holds that pain just is a certain kind of neural activity, as lightning just is electrical discharge.

vocabulary.definition: The view that mental states are nothing more than behavior or dispositions to behave.
vocabulary.example: A behaviorist analyzes 'Sam is thirsty' as 'Sam would drink if offered water.'

vocabulary.definition: The view that thinking is computation: the rule-governed manipulation of symbols sensitive to their form.
vocabulary.example: On the computational theory of mind, solving a math problem in your head is running a kind of program.

vocabulary.definition: Fodor's hypothesis that thinking occurs in an inner symbolic system with words and grammar, sometimes called Mentalese.
vocabulary.example: On the language of thought hypothesis, believing that dogs bark involves a mental sentence built from symbols for dogs and barking.

vocabulary.definition: The qualitative, felt characters of conscious experiences, such as the way red looks or pain feels.
vocabulary.example: Two people may agree that a tomato is red yet, the inverted spectrum worry suggests, have different qualia.

vocabulary.definition: The objection that a system could have the full functional organization of a mind while having no conscious experiences at all.
vocabulary.example: Block's China Brain is a famous absent qualia case.

thinkingExercise.title: Write a Machine Table for an Emotion
thinkingExercise.prompt: Try to define a mental state purely by its functional role, and see where the definition strains.
steps: Choose an emotion such as jealousy, boredom or fear. List its typical causes (situations, perceptions, other mental states).
List its typical effects: on other mental states (beliefs, desires, attention) and on behavior.
Check your definition against an octopus, a robot and a person who hides their feelings. Does your functional role fit all the cases you think it should, and only those?
Now ask: does your definition capture what the emotion feels like? Describe what, if anything, is left out.
Imagine a system that met your definition exactly. Would you be confident it felt the emotion? Write a short reply to Block from a functionalist's point of view.

summary: Behaviorism failed because mental states produce behavior only in combination with other mental states; the identity theory failed to allow that creatures with different brains could share mental states.
Putnam's multiple realizability argument led to functionalism: mental states are defined by their causal roles, like the states of a machine table, and can be realized in many physical systems.
The computational theory of mind holds that thinking is symbol manipulation; Fodor's language of thought hypothesis appeals to productivity, systematicity and the mechanization of reasoning.

The inverted spectrum and Block's China Brain suggest that functional role may not fix conscious experience; replies include accepting the China Brain's consciousness, denying absent qualia are possible, and limiting functionalism to non-conscious states.
Putnam later rejected functionalism over the triviality of implementation, and others questioned multiple realizability, but the view remains central to cognitive science and to debates about AI.

quiz.question: What is the main objection to the mind-brain identity theory from multiple realizability?
options: Brains are too complex to study
It implies that creatures with different nervous systems, like octopuses, could not share our mental states
It implies dualism
It cannot explain behavior
quiz.explanation: If pain is identical to a specific human brain state, any creature lacking that state cannot be in pain, which seems presumptuous.

quiz.question: Why did behaviorism fail to define mental states in terms of behavior alone?
options: Because mental states produce behavior only in combination with other mental states
Because behavior cannot be observed
Because animals do not behave
Because Descartes refuted it
quiz.explanation: A thirsty person who believes the water is poisoned will not drink, so any behavioral definition of thirst has to mention other mental states.

quiz.question: According to functionalism, whether a state is a pain depends on the role it plays, not on the material it is made of.
quiz.explanation: Like a mousetrap, a mental state is defined by what it does, so it could in principle be realized in neurons, silicon or something else.

quiz.question: Fodor's argument from systematicity points out that:
options: Thoughts are always true
Brains are like computers in their hardware
Anyone who can think 'John loves Mary' can also think 'Mary loves John'
Thoughts cannot be expressed in language
quiz.explanation: Thoughts come in structured families, which suggests they are built from reusable symbolic parts, as in a language of thought.

quiz.question: In Block's China Brain, what is the population of China supposed to do?
options: Vote on what a robot should think
Simulate the functional organization of a human brain using radios
Calculate pi
Imagine colors
quiz.explanation: If the nation as a whole implements a brain's functional organization, functionalism implies it has mental states, which many find absurd for experiences.

quiz.question: The inverted spectrum idea was first raised by John Locke.
quiz.explanation: In his Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Locke imagined that the color experience a violet gives one person might be the one a marigold gives another.

quiz.question: Shoemaker's reply to the absent qualia objection is that:
options: The China Brain is obviously unconscious
Qualia do not exist
Consciousness is non-physical
Qualia make a functional difference by causing beliefs about experience, so they cannot be absent from a functional duplicate
quiz.explanation: If qualia have causal roles, including causing our beliefs about them, a perfect functional duplicate must have them too.

quiz.question: Hilary Putnam remained a committed defender of functionalism throughout his career.
quiz.explanation: In Representation and Reality (1988), Putnam rejected functionalism, arguing that any sufficiently complex system can be described as implementing almost any computation.

quiz.question: Researchers find that a language model has internal states tracking the positions of pieces in a board game it only ever saw as lists of moves. A functionalist would most naturally say this is:
options: Proof that the model is conscious
Irrelevant, because the model is not made of neurons
Evidence of states that play a representational role, relevant to whether it has beliefs
A refutation of multiple realizability
quiz.explanation: For functionalists, what matters is whether a state plays the right role. Representation is part of that, though belief also requires broader integration, and consciousness is a further question.

goDeeper.body:
David Chalmers offered a powerful argument in favor of a functionalist view of consciousness, even though he is famous for the hard problem (Day 84). In *The Conscious Mind* (1996), he defended the **principle of organizational invariance**: any two systems with the same fine-grained functional organization will have the same conscious experiences. His argument is the **fading qualia** thought experiment.

Imagine replacing your neurons one at a time with silicon chips that perform exactly the same function, receiving and sending the same signals. At the end, you are entirely silicon. Suppose that silicon systems lack experience. Then at some point along the way your experiences must have faded or vanished. But your functional organization never changed, so you would go on behaving and *believing* exactly as before. You would say "My experience of this red is as vivid as ever" while it was in fact fading to grey. Chalmers argued it is very implausible that a rational being could be so systematically wrong about its own experience. So the qualia must remain, and organizational invariance holds.

This is significant because Chalmers is not a physicalist: he thinks consciousness is not fully explained by physical facts. Yet he holds that consciousness is lawfully tied to functional organization, which means a perfect silicon simulation of a brain would be conscious. Critics respond that the argument assumes what is at issue, or that experience might vanish abruptly at some threshold. Others, such as the biologically minded neuroscientist Anil Seth, suspect that consciousness depends on properties of living systems, such as metabolism and self-maintenance, that a silicon replacement might lack. The thought experiment remains one of the key pivots in the debate over whether machines could ever be conscious.

questions: If an octopus and a human can both be in pain, what exactly do their pains have in common?
Would the China Brain be conscious? What would it take to convince you either way?
Could a system have beliefs without having any conscious experience at all?
